Below is the screenshot of the post, which garnered more than 475K views: Investigation The Desk started its investigation by doing a Google search with the keyword "asteroid to hit Earth in Jan," The search results led the Desk to an article by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), posted on Jan 25. The article stated that a "small" near-Earth asteroid – 2023 BU – will "zoom over the southern tip of South America at about 4:27 p.m. PST (7:27 p.m. EST) only 2,200 miles (3,600 kilometers) above the planet's surface and well within the orbit of geosynchronous satellites." Notably, the NASA article mentioned the asteroid as "small," with its size estimated to be 11.5 to 28 feet (3.5 to 8.5 meters) across. This was in contrast to the article shared in the Twitter post, which mentioned the asteroid 2023 BU as "huge." Here is the link to the article , and below is the screenshot of the same: The Desk found another article by the Space.com website, which reported on Jan 27 that the asteroid zoomed past the Earth in a close shave. The article's headline read: "Watch an SUV-sized asteroid zoom by Earth in close shave flyby in this time-lapse video." The article included a time-lapse video of the telescopic view of the rock when it was 22,000 km from the closest point on Earth's surface. Here is the link to the article , and below is the screenshot of the same: In the subsequent investigation step, the Desk conducted a Google search with the keyword "asteroid 2023 BU zooms past Earth". The results led us to an article by BBC posted on Jan 27. The article titled "Asteroid 2023 BU: Space rock passes closer than some satellites" reported that the asteroid was of the size of a minibus whipped over the southern tip of South America just before 00:30 am GMT. Here is the link to the article , and below is its screenshot: The Desk then went through the article shared in the Twitter post and found it mentioned that the asteroid will "shoot past the planet on Friday, January 27 at 12.30 am." "According to NASA's space experts, asteroids smaller than 82ft are more than likely to burn in the Earth's atmosphere as opposed to hitting the ground," the article read. The Desk then conducted a Google search to establish how the asteroids were classified as vast and small, and we found an article by NASA explaining about asteroids. "Asteroids range in size from Vesta – the largest at about 329 miles (530 kilometers) in diameter – to bodies that are less than 33 feet (10 meters) across. The total mass of all the asteroids combined is less than that of Earth's Moon," the article stated, establishing that the asteroid 2023 BU was small and not huge. Here is the link to the article , and below is its screenshot: The Desk also found an article by The National which reported about Asteroid 2023 BU zooming past the Earth's surface on at 00:27 GMT on Jan 27. The headline of the article posted on Jan 27 read: "Asteroid 2023 BU in 'extraordinarily close' call with Earth". Here is the link to the article and below is the screenshot of the same: Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the asteroid went past the Earth's surface in a close encounter, and didn't come in contact with it.

title: PTI Fact Check: Digitally altered video clip of TV news anchor shared on social media with false claim
content: New Delhi, Jan 30 (Abhinav Gupta / Pratyush Ranjan PTI Fact Check ): An Instagram user shared a video of Hindi news channel anchor Anjana Om Kashyap claiming she sang a Bollywood song during a live broadcast on the TV channel. The PTI Fact Check found in its investigation that the video was digitally altered to make it look like she was singing a Hindi movie song. The Instagram Reel with the edited video was shared on social media with a false claim. Claim An Instagram user shared an Instagram Reel of Hindi news anchor Anjana Om Kashyap purportedly singing a Bollywood song during a live show. The text in the Reel posted on Jan 8 read: "Anajana loves to sing on the LIVE broadcast." Here are the links to the post and its archive post . Below is the screenshot of the post, which has garnered over 3 lakh likes so far: Investigation The Desk started its investigation with an InVid Tool search on the video and found a few keyframes. A separate Google search on one of them led the Desk to a YouTube video posted by the official channel of Aaj Tak. The headline of the 7:37-minute video posted on June 30 last year read: "Halla Bol: राहुल के नाम पर भड़कीं सुप्रिया श्रीनेत | Anjana Om Kashyap | Maharashtra Political Crisis" (Halla Bol: Supriya Shrinate got angry in the name of Rahul. Anjana Om Kashyap | Maharashtra Political Crisis). Here is the link to the video , and below is the screenshot of the same: The Desk noticed that the news anchor's dress and the badge design on her blazer in the YouTube video were the same as in the Instagram Reel. Below is a comparison of the two: The Desk noticed that Anjana had done several shows on the Aaj Tak channel wearing the same dress. Hence, we couldn't establish from which video the clip was taken to be used in the Reel. In the subsequent investigation step, the Desk oversaw the Instagram Reel and noticed that the lip movement was not in sync with the song running in the background. We also noticed that the channel logo was digitally altered, and the name of "आज तक" was changed to "खाज तक." The Instagram user also mentioned his name under it. Below is a screenshot of the same: We then scanned the page of the Instagram user 'Perfect Whistler,' with over 20,000 followers, and found it had shared several digitally altered videos of political leaders. Here is the link to the page and the screenshot of the same: Earlier, the Desk had recently debunked one such edited video: All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen Asaduddin Owaisi was allegedly shown singing a religious hymn. Here is the link to the article: PTI Fact Check: Digitally altered video clip of Asaduddin Owaisi's speech shared on social media with false claim Subsequently, the Desk concluded that a digitally altered video clip of news anchor Anjana Om Kashyap was shared in social media post with a false claim. The Desk reached out to the anchor for comment, and the copy will be updated with her quotes if available.

title: PTI Fact Check: 'Coronavirus' not a Latin word but combines two Latin terms; Facebook post calling it 'heart attack virus' misleading
content: New Delhi, Jan 31 (Abhinav Gupta / Pratyush Ranjan PTI Fact Check ): A Facebook user shared a video that claimed that 'Coronavirus' is a Latin term, and it means 'heart attack virus' if translated into English using Google Translate. The PTI Fact Check Desk found in its investigation that Coronavirus is not a Latin word but a combination of two Latin terms, and they don't translate into 'heart attack virus' in English. The claim in the video shared in the Facebook post is misleading. Claim In the Facebook video dated Jan 6, which garnered over 300 likes and over 450 shares, a woman was seen using Google Translation, setting it from Latin to English, and entered 'coronavirus' in three separate words using one space between the first two words and two spaces between the second and the third word in Google translate. It appeared like "Cor(One space)ona(Two spaces)virus, and Google translated it into English as "heart attack virus." The woman said in the Facebook video: "There's a coincidence, and there's a coincidence, but this is weird! Let me show you something. Go to Google Translate and select Latin to English. In the Latin version, you just put 'cor' in one space, 'one,' two spaces, 'virus,' and would you know what it says – (indicating to translated text – 'heart attack virus')? Do you think that's just a coincidence? Try it out on your computer and see what you think. We were always told it was just a respiratory disease. Still think it's a coincidence there are so many people getting a heart attack?" (Sic). Here is the link and the archive link to the Facebook post. Below is the screenshot of the page: Investigation As claimed in the video, the Desk started the investigation using Google Translate. First, the Desk selected 'Latin to English' in the Google Translate app and typed 'coronavirus' in the box for Latin words. The app translated this as 'The coronavirus' in English. You can see the screenshot of the page below- We found that the term's meaning remained the same when translated from Latin to English using Google Translate. Subsequently, the Desk entered the words described in the video ('Cor ona virus'), and its meaning in English changed to 'heart attack virus.' Below is the screenshot of the page- While the desired result was based on syllables being put in a specific format, the Desk tried Google Translate by first reducing the two spaces to one space between the second and the third word 'ona' and 'virus.' The search results gave "cor ona virus" in English. Also, "Cor ona," with one space between the two words, translates to "heart wave," Google suggested translating the word from Portuguese instead of Latin. This means that the claim in the video that the word 'Coronavirus,' which was termed as a Latin word in the video, becomes 'heart attack virus' in English only when the syllables are put in a specific manner in Google Translate. In the subsequent investigation step, the Desk searched the term 'Coronavirus' to know the word's origin. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention , "Coronaviruses are named for the crown-like spikes on their surface." According to the Merriam-Webster dictionary, Coronavirus combines two Latin terms, ' Corona ' and ' Virus '. Corona is Latin for crown, and Virus is Latin for poison. According to the documented etymology of the word Coronavirus, it was first used in a short article published in the 1968 edition of Nature , a scientific journal. While corona and virus were Latin terms, the Desk found that "cor" was a Latin term for 'heart.' However, "ona" did not mean anything in Latin. Also, there was no specific Latin term for 'heart attack.' According to the World Health Organisation , the Coronavirus disease (COVID-19) is an infectious disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. On why Google Translate gave the result as 'heart attack virus' only when syllables were typed in a specific manner, the Desk read the Disclaimer section of Google Translate. "Reasonable efforts have been made to provide an accurate translation. However, no automated translation is perfect nor intended to replace human translators. Translations are provided as a service to users of the <company name> website and are provided "as is." No warranty of any kind, either expressed or implied, is made regarding the accuracy, reliability, or correctness of any translations made from <source language> into any other language. Some content (such as images, videos, Flash, etc.) may not be accurately translated due to the limitations of the translation software," the disclaimer read. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that 'Coronavirus' was not a Latin term. Its translation to 'heart attack virus,' as shown by the woman in the Facebook video, was based on a specific three-part word split.

title: PTI Fact Check: Edited photo of Indian cricket fan with placard supporting Pakistan's Babar Azam shared on social media as recent
content: New Delhi, Feb 01 (Abhinav Gupta / Pratyush Ranjan PTI Fact Check ): A Twitter user shared a photo of an Indian cricket fan, purportedly holding a placard supporting Pakistani captain Babar Azam over Virat Kohli. The user also claimed that the image was of Ranchi, where the first of the three-match T20I series between India and New Zealand was held recently. The PTI Fact Check Desk found in its investigation that the photo was from the 11th season of the Indian Premier League (IPL) in 2018, and the text on the placard was edited. The morphed photo was shared on social media as recently with a false claim. Claim A Twitter user shared a photo of an Indian cricket fan, purportedly holding a placard in support of Pakistani skipper Babar Azam over Virat Kohli. The user mentioned the image was from Ranchi, indicating it was from the recent T20 match between India and New Zealand, which was held there. "Sorry Virat sir, but Babar Ajam is God of Cricket for me… #7," the placard in the photo read. "Babar Azam fan in Ranchi India…," read the tweet, posted on Jan 27, which has garnered over 27,000 views and nearly 200 likes. Here are the links to the post and the archive post , and below is its screenshot: Investigation The Desk started the investigation with a Google Reverse Image search on the photo shared in the Twitter post. The results led us to another tweet posted on Jan 27, which carried the same picture and claim. Here are the links to the Twitter post and its archive post , and below is its screenshot: The Desk found another tweet dating back to Jul 7, 2020, which carried a similar photo with the placard displaying a different text. The text on the placard read: "Sorry Sachin Sir, but MS Dhoni is God of Cricket for me… #7". The Twitter post read: "Sorry Sachin, But MS Dhoni is GOD OF CRICKET" #HappyBirthdayDhoni | @msdhoni." Here is the link to the post , and below is its screenshot: In the next step of the investigation, the Desk conducted a Google search on the photo with the keyword "MS Dhoni God of Cricket," which led us to a news report by DNA posted on Apr 21, 2018. The news report, titled "IPL 2018: Watch- fan touches MS Dhoni's feet during CSK v/s RR match", was related to an incident during the eleventh season of IPL in 2018 when a fan ran into the ground to touch MS Dhoni's feet. The article's featured image, however, was the photo of the placard reading: "Sorry Sachin Sir, but MS Dhoni is God of Cricket for me… #7." Here is the link to the report , and below is the screenshot of the same: Assuming that the photo was initially clicked in 2018, the Desk conducted an advanced search on Google with a specific set of keywords which led us to a report by ESPN Cricinfo. The article – the report of the IPL match between Mumbai Indians and Royal Challengers Bangalore played at Wankhede Stadium on Apr 17, 2018 – carried the original photo. Here is the link to the article , and below is the screenshot of the same: The Desk also noticed that the text on the placard in the photo shared on Twitter mentioned #7, which was Dhoni's jersey number. Babar Azam's jersey number, on the other hand, is 56. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that an edited photo of an Indian fan was shared on social media to make it look like he held a placard to support Pakistani cricketer Babar Azam over Virat Kohli.

title: PTI Fact Check: Selected part of Bollywood actor Ranbir Kapoor's promotional video shoot shared on social media as real
content: New Delhi, Feb 01 (Abhinav Gupta / Pratyush Ranjan PTI Fact Check ): A Twitter user shared a video claiming Bollywood actor Ranbir Kapoor threw away a fan's phone in anger. The PTI Fact Check Desk found in its investigation that the video was a part of a smartphone company's ad campaign for a new phone. The video was shared as an actual incident on social media with a false claim. Claim A Twitter user shared a video of Ranbir Kapoor purportedly throwing away a man's phone who was trying to click a selfie with him. "Must look forward to this behaviour of angry Ranbir Kapoor #angryranbirkapoor," read the tweet posted on Jan 27. Here are the link and archive link to the tweet, and below is a screenshot of the same: Investigation The Desk noticed that the video was from Bollywood photographer Viral Bhayani. We clicked on the hyperlink and found a tweet by Bhayani posted on Jan 27 with a similar claim. Here is the link and archive link of the tweet, which has received over 475K views, 1700 likes, and over 300 retweets. In the subsequent investigation step, the Desk went through the comment section and found many users claiming it was an ad promotion, not an actual incident. One of the users shared a tweet from Oppo's official Twitter handle with the same video, shot from a different angle. Oppo India's tweet, posted on Jan 29, which has garnered over 24K views, read: "Just in case you've missed it, #RanbirKapoor hands a fan an upgrade of a lifetime with the new #OPPOReno8T. The new OPPO RENO 8T strikes the perfect balance between immersive visuals & a relaxed grip for an all-around premium experience, Releasing Feb 3rd. #AStepAbove" Here is the link and archive link to the tweet: We also found another tweet by OPPO India just before a day of viral video with the caption "Why did Ranbir throw a fan's phone? Tweet #AStepAbove to reveal exclusive footage." Here is the link and archive link of the tweet posted on Jan 28. Below is the screenshot of the tweet: Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the video showing Ranbir Kapoor throwing away a fan's phone out of anger was an ad campaign by Oppo India. The video was shared in social media posts as an actual incident with a false claim.

title: PTI Fact Check: Dubai Ruler's order to rename district as 'Hind City' not related to India or the Hindu community; Social media posts shared with the misleading claim
content: New Delhi, Feb 02 (Abhinav Gupta / Pratyush Ranjan PTI Fact Check ): BJP national spokesperson RP Singh shared a Twitter post claiming UAE Prime Minister and Ruler of Dubai Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum had ordered the renaming of Al Minhad district and its surrounding areas as 'Hind City' allegedly to "honour the contribution of India and Hindus towards humanity." The PTI Fact Check Desk found in its investigation that the Ruler of Dubai's order to rename the place had nothing to do with India or Hindus. 'Hind' has several meanings in Arabic and is also an old female Arabic name. The social media post was shared with a misleading claim. Claim BJP national spokesperson RP Singh shared a photo of UAE PM and Dubai Ruler Sheikha Hind bint Maktoum bin Juma Al Maktoum along with the claim that he issued the order to rename Al Minhad district and its surrounding areas as 'Hind City.' Singh claimed that he gave the order to "honour the contribution of India and Hindus towards humanity." "Ruler of Dubai and PM of UAE, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum has ordered that a district in the emirate be renamed. Al Minhad and its surrounding 84 Square KM areas will now be known as "Hind City" to honour the contribution of India and Hindus towards humanity," read the post, dated Jan 30, which has garnered over 6,600 views to date. Here are the links to the Twitter post and its archive post and below is the screenshot of the same: Investigation The Desk started the investigation with a Google search on the claim of the UAE PM issuing an order to rename the district of Al Minhad and its nearby areas. The results led to another tweet dated Jan 30, which carried the same claim. Here are the links to the tweet , which has garnered 1.6 million views to date with nearly 40K likes and 8,000 retweets, and the archive post . BJP spokesperson and MP made a similar Twitter claim from Uttarakhand Anil Baluni. "Al Minhad city in Dubai has been renamed as 'Hind City' by PM of Dubai Sheikh Mohammed Rashid. Under the dynamic leadership of PM Shri @narendramodi ji, India's respect, and honor have increased tremendously on the world stage. #ModiHaiToMumkinHai" read his tweet dated Jan 31, which over 3,200 people have read. Here are the links to the post and its archive post and below is its screenshot: The Desk subsequently found a report by the India Today website, posted on Jan 31, whose headline read: "UAE's Sheikh Mohammed Al Maktoum renames Al Minhad as 'Hind City.'" As per the report, Maktoum issued the order on Sunday (Jan 29). The Al Minhad area includes four zones - Hind 1, Hind 2, Hind 3, and Hind 4, spread over 83.9km. Here is the link to the report and below is the screenshot of the same: Another website named the Gulf News also reported Al Maktoum's order to rename the Al Minhad area without mentioning India, Hindus, or PM Modi. Here is the link to the report dated Jan 29 and below is its screenshot: The Desk found several other reports in the Indian media, which carried the news of the renaming of the Al Minhad district. However, none of the words mentioned after whose name the area was renamed or the reason behind the order by the UAE PM. The reports by Navbharat Times and Republic World can be viewed here and here . Notably, none of the reports mentioned India, Hindus, or Prime Minister Narendra Modi behind UAE PM's order to rename the district. Continuing our search regarding the claim made in social media posts, the Desk found an official announcement on the Government of Dubai's Media Office's official website. Like news articles, the official announcement also reported about the order to rename the Al Minhad area as "Hind City" without any mention of India or Hindus or PM Modi. Here is the link to the report and below is its screenshot: Notably, UAE PM and Dubai Ruler Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum's senior wife's name is Sheikha Hind bint Maktoum bin Juma Al Maktoum. The Desk contacted Dubai Government's Media Office by e-mail for its comment. A response was awaited till the time of publishing this article. While we could not establish the reason behind the UAE PM's order to rename the Al Minhad area, it was concluded that the claim shared in the viral tweets was false.

title: PTI Fact Check: 43-second video clip from Bengal Muslim cleric's speech footage shared on social media with misleading claim
content: New Delhi, Feb 04 (Abhinav Gupta / Pratyush Ranjan PTI Fact Check ): A Twitter user shared a 43-second video clip of a speech by Pirzada Taha Siddiqui of Furfura Sharif in West Bengal's Hooghly, claiming he allegedly incited Muslims to prepare their children to 'wage war against Hindus'. The PTI Fact Check Desk found in its investigation that a selected part of an extended version of his speech was taken out of context and shared in social media posts with a misleading claim. The claim in the tweet was misleading. Claim A Twitter user shared a video clip of a speech by Pirzada Taha Siddiqui of Furfura Sharif in West Bengal's Hooghly and claimed that he allegedly incited Muslims to prepare their children to 'wage war against Hindus'. "The person in the video is none other than Peerzada Taha Siddiqui of Furfura Sharif, Hooghly.. He urged his community to prepare their children for war against Hindus. Provocative hate speeches targeting Hindus are increasing by the day, but how long will these go unnoticed. (Sic)", read the tweet dated Feb 2, which garnered over 57K views, nearly 700 likes, and 475 retweets. In the 43-second video shared in the tweet, Taha Siddiqui was seen addressing in the Bangla language. "Hey Muslims, wake up! Hey Muslims, teach your sons and daughters to fight; teach them to wage war. Get ready! Be present! Present the sons and daughters of Muslims. Fathers and mothers, get your sons and daughters ready. We have to fight a war against Hindus. We have to fight against Hindus", read the English translation of his speech in Bangla. Here are the links to the post and its archive post , and below is the screenshot of the same: Investigation The Desk started the investigation with an InVid Tool search on the video, which provided a few keyframes of the footage. A separate Google search on one of the six keyframes led the Desk to another tweet, which carried the same video clip with a similar claim. "Peerzada Taha Siddiqui of Furfura Sharif mazaar, #Bengal, exhorts Ms to prepare their children for war against Hs. Secularism in Air ? Does the Bengal government @MamataOfficial have the courage to take action? @SuvenduWB @tathagata2 @Pushpendraamu," read the tweet dated Feb 1, which garnered over 3200 views and 40 likes. Here are the links to the post and its archive post , and below is the screenshot of the same: The Desk conducted a customised Google search with relevant keywords and found a 27:37-minute video posted by a YouTube channel named 'Waz Mehfil 21' on Jan 27 this year. The title of the YouTube video in Bengali, posted on Jan 27, roughly translated to English as: "Be prepared to fight | Pirzada Toha Siddiqui | Pirzada Toha Siddiqui will roar like a tiger." When we compared the 43-second video with the YouTube video, we found that the footage shared on Twitter was a part of the extended version posted on YouTube. At the 15:40-minute counter in the YouTube video, Siddiqui can be heard making the same statement as was in the Twitter video. "Hey Muslims, wake up! Hey Muslims, teach your sons and daughters to fight; teach them to wage war. Get ready! Be present! Present the sons and daughters of Muslims. Fathers and mothers, get your sons and daughters ready. We have to fight a war against Hindus. We have to fight against Hindus," he said between 15:40 minutes and 16:23 minutes in the YouTube Video. The Desk noticed that only this part was clipped and shared on Twitter with a misleading claim. However, after 16:23 minutes, Siddiqui explained that the war should be over education and not with weapons. "After saying this, I can see the fear on all ministers' faces. They think I am here to spark a communal fire. I reiterate, Muslims, get your children ready to fight Hindus and Christians. But the war must not be fought with swords, guns, and lathis. That war will be fought over education. A Muslim boy will compete with a Hindu boy over education, and a Muslim girl will compete with a Hindu girl over education. As they progress, Bengal's Hindus and Muslims will unite and fight with education as their weapon," he said, continuing his speech after 16:23 minutes in the video. Here is the link to the video , and below is its screenshot: Subsequently, the Desk concluded that a smaller part of the video of Pirzada Taha Siddiqui's speech in Hooghly was taken out of context and used in social media posts with a misleading claim.

title: PTI Fact Check: Pakistan wrestler's video shared in name of Dhirendra Shastri of Bageshwar Dham on social media with false claim
content: New Delhi, Feb 05 (Abhinav Gupta / Pratyush Ranjan PTI Fact Check ): A video of two wrestlers was shared on a Facebook page claiming the one who pinned the other wrestler was Dhirendra Krishna Shastri, the self-styled godman from the Bageshwar Dham temple. The PTI Fact Check Desk found in its investigation that the wrestler who knocked down another wrestler was Pakistan's Ghulam Hussain Pathan. The claim in the social media post was false. Claim A Facebook page shared a video of a duel between two wrestlers claiming one of them was Dhirendra Krishna Shastri of Bageshwar Dham Temple. "बाबा बागेश्वर का अनोखा वीडियो वायरल #Bageshwardham #bageshwar (Unique video of Baba Bageshwar goes viral #Bageshwardham #bageshwar)," read the caption of the 15-second video, posted on Jan 23. Here are the links to the post and its archive post , and below is the screenshot of the same: Investigation The Desk started its investigation with an InVid Tool search on the video, which provided a few keyframes of the footage. A Google search on one of the six keyframes led the Desk to a Twitter post carrying the same video with a similar claim. "अखाड़े में भी धोबी पछाड़- बागेश्वर धाम के पुजारी, पंडित धीरेंद्र कृष्ण शास्त्री अखाड़े में कैसे धोबी पछाड़ मारते हैं, देख लीजिए. #BageshwarDhamSarkar," read the post dated Jan 29. "See how Bageshwar Dham priest Pandit Dhirendra Krishna Shastri slams in the arena," read the post when roughly translated to English. Here are the links to the post and its archive post , and below is the screenshot of the same: The Desk subsequently found a YouTube video, a more extended version of the one shared in social media posts. The video was posted by Sachal TV, a verified YouTube channel with 254K subscribers, on Nov 6, 2020. The headline of the 2:19-minute video read: "New Sindhi Malakhra Ghulam Hussain Pathan." Here is the link to the video , and below is the screenshot of the same: We compared some keyframes of the two videos – one shared on social media and the other posted on YouTube – and found them to be the same. Taking a cue from this, the Desk conducted a Google search for the keyword "Ghulam Hussain Pathan wrestler." The results led us to several YouTube videos if the wrestler. Three of them can be viewed here , here , and here . The Desk also noticed that the headline of the YouTube video by Sachal TV mentioned the term 'Malakhra.' We found that Malakhra or Malakhro is a traditional form of wrestling in Sindh, Pakistan. The Desk then conducted a Google search on specific keywords on the wrestler, which led us to images on Shutterstock. The photos of the wrestler were posted along with the caption: "Wrestler Ghulam Hussain Pathan fights his opponent during the traditional Sindhi Malakhra wrestling in Karachi, Pakistan." Here is the link to the Shutterstock page , and below is the screenshot of the same: The Desk also found a news interview of Pathan with NTV News HD. The interview was posted on YouTube on Feb 21, 2020. "Ghulam Hussain Pahlwan is a young and famous pahlwan in Sindh Pakistan. Ghulam Hussain Pahlwan interview at Pashtoon student festival in Karachi with NTV News HD," read the video's description. Here is the link to the YouTube video , and below is its screenshot: Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the wrestler in the video shared in social media posts was not Dhirendra Krishna Shastri but a Pakistani named Ghulam Hussain Pathan.

title: PTI Fact Check: 2022 photo of Shah Rukh Khan from the sets of his next film 'Jawan' shared as recent on social media
content: New Delhi, Feb 06 (Abhinav Gupta / Pratyush Ranjan PTI Fact Check ): A Twitter user shared Shah Rukh Khan's photo claiming it was his recent picture from the sets of his upcoming film 'Jawan.' The PTI Fact Check Desk found in its investigation that it was almost a year-old photo but shared as recent on social media with a misleading claim. Claim A Twitter user shared a photo of Shah Rukh Khan, claiming it was a recent look of the Bollywood actor from the sets of his upcoming Bollywood film 'Jawan.' "#SRK back on the sets of #Jawan today in his monster avatar," read the Tweet post on Jan 31, which garnered over 155K views and 5500 likes. Here are the links to the post and its archive post , and below is the screenshot of the same: Investigation The Desk started the investigation with a customised Google Reverse Image search on the photo. The search results led us to a report by the Times of India, dated Apr 7, 2022. The report carried the same photo and its distant shot and titled the article: "Exclusive photos: Shah Rukh Khan shoots for his next helmed by director Atlee in the city." Here is the link to the report , and below is the screenshot of the same: The Desk noticed that the report had mentioned the name of the photographer below the pictures as Himanshu Shinde. In the next part of the investigation, the Desk scanned the Instagram handle of Shah Rukh Khan and found two posts related to 'Jawan' published in June last year. The posts – a photo and teaser of the film – also showed Khan wrapped in bandages, as seen in the pic shared on social media. The posts can be viewed here and here . Below are the screenshots of the Instagram posts: The Desk then reached out to Himanshu Shinde, a photojournalist with Times of India, who confirmed to PTI that the photo was clicked by him on April 17, 2022. "The photo was clicked on April 17 last year. SRK was not driving the ambulance. He was just sitting on the driver's seat. It was a scene of his movie Jawan," he told PTI. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that Shah Rukh Khan's photo shared as recent from the sets of his upcoming film 'Jawan' dates back to April 2022.

title: PTI Fact Check: Starbucks CEO's 2013 quote on traditional marriage twisted and shared in social media posts with misleading claim
content: New Delhi, Feb 07 (Abhinav Gupta / Pratyush Ranjan PTI Fact Check ): A Twitter user shared a screenshot of an article where long-time Starbucks CEO and current interim CEO Howard Schultz allegedly said, "If you support traditional marriage, don't buy our coffee." The PTI Fact Check Desk found in its investigation that a statement made by Schultz in a 2013 annual general meeting of the company had been misconstrued and shared in social media posts with a misleading claim. Claim A Twitter user shared a post on Jan 26 with the screenshot of an article that quoted long-time Starbucks CEO and current interim CEO Howard Schultz said, "if you support traditional marriage, don't buy our coffee." The post has garnered 165.8K views, over 2000 likes and 1100 retweets. Here are the links to the post and archive post and a screenshot of the same- Investigation The Desk started its investigation with a Google Reverse Image Search on the image posted by the Twitter user, which led us to another Twitter post from Jan 27 with the same screenshot of the article with 36.2K views and 587 likes. Here are links to the post and archive post ; a screenshot is below. Taking a cue from the screenshot, the Desk conducted a Google search for the keyword "Starbucks CEO on traditional marriage". The search results led the Desk to a YouTube video posted on Nov 2, 2013. The 4:39-minute video was titled: "Starbucks' CEO Howard Schultz On Gay Rights And Companies' Social Responsibilities". At 1:20 minutes in the video, Schultz said: "When I made those statements, our stock was up 38 per cent for the year. I said something with great respect and civility to that shareholder who was not in favour of providing same-sex benefits to partners who were gay, and all I said to him was that we believe in respect and dignity for all people. The company's results demonstrate they were on the right side of that debate." We listened to the complete interview, but nowhere did Schultz make the statement as quoted in the screenshot. Here is the link to the video , and below is its screenshot: Continuing its search, the Desk found a 2013 article by Forbes with the headline "Howard Schultz to Anti-Gay-Marriage Starbucks Shareholder: 'You Can Sell Your Shares". According to the report, when a shareholder complained to Schulz about "disappointing" earnings due to the company's support of gay marriage, the CEO responded, "Not every decision is an economic decision. Even though you recite statistics that are narrow in time, we did provide a 38% shareholder return over the last year. I don't know how many things you invest in, but I suspect not many companies, products, or investments have returned 38% over the last 12 months. It is not an economic decision to me. The lens through which we are making that decision is the lens of our people. We employ over 200,000 people in this company and want to embrace diversity. Of all kinds." Here is the link to the report and below is the screenshot- The shareholder meeting occurred after the Supreme Court struck down a section of the Defense of Marriage Act that denied federal benefits to couples in same-sex marriages in 2013. A customised keyword search in Google led us to a June 2015 article by Starbucks titled "Starbucks Applauds Supreme Court's Ruling on Marriage Equality". Here is the link to the article , and below is its screenshot: Subsequently, the Desk concluded that Schultz – who has a long history with Starbucks and returned last year to lead the company as CEO on an interim basis – never made the remark which was shared in the tweet recently. His stand on same-sex marriage was misconstrued over time and shared in social media posts with a misleading claim. The Desk reached out to Starbucks by email for its comment. The copy will be updated as soon as we receive a reply to the mail.

title: PTI Fact Check: 2017 photo of protest against Adani Group in Australia shared as recent with misleading claim on social media
content: New Delhi, Feb 07 (Abhinav Gupta / Pratyush Ranjan PTI Fact Check ): A Twitter user shared a photo of a purported protest against Indian conglomerate Adani group and claimed it took place in Australia recently. The claim comes in the wake of the upheaval in India after New York-based investor research firm Hindenburg Research allegedly accused the Gautam Adani-led conglomerate of 'stock manipulation and financial irregularities' over the course of decades. The PTI Fact Check Desk found in its investigation that the photo shared recently was six years old and shared in social media posts with a misleading claim. Claim A Twitter user shared a photo on Feb 1, which showed a group of people carrying a placard stating "#Stop Adani." The post, which garnered over 556.9K views and 6600 likes, read: "Why Adani's Fall Makes Many Happy! Protest against Adani in Australia." Here are the links to the post and its archive post , and below is the screenshot of the same- Investigation The Desk started the investigation with a Google Reverse Image search on the photo and found another Twitter post, which carried the same picture and claim. Here are the links to the post and its archive post , and below is its screenshot- Continuing its search, the Desk found a report by a website, stopadani.com, which described itself as "the biggest grassroots movement in Australia's history to stop Adani's coal mine." On the website, multiple people were seen carrying placards with the hashtag "Stop Adani", similar to the one seen on the Twitter post. Here is the link to the website , and below is the screenshot of the same: The Desk then conducted a Google search for the keyword "protest against Adani in Australia, coal mine" and found a 2017 tweet from a verified user carrying the same picture as that in the Twitter post. Here is the link , the archive link , and the screenshot of the tweet: Continuing its search, the Desk found a 2017 report on a website "about regional," carrying the same picture as the one in the tweets, with the headline "Hundreds protested against the coal mining Adani at Congo Beach, Eurobodalla." Here is the link , the archive link , and the screengrab of the report. The Google search also led the Desk to reports by The Wire and The Guardian on the protest in Australia against Adani Group's coal mining project in 2017. Also, with the Adani Group grabbing headlines recently over the Hindenburg report, news organizations would have covered such protests in Australia. However, no such coverage recently was found in Google search.

title: PTI Fact Check: No, these four videos not related to Feb 6 Turkiye-Syria earthquakes; Old and unrelated footage shared on social media with false claims
content: New Delhi, Feb 07 (Abhinav Gupta / Pratyush Ranjan PTI Fact Check ): Social media platforms have been flooded with harrowing visuals claiming they are from Turkiye, formerly Turkey, and Syria, which were rocked by a series of devastating earthquakes on Feb 6, killing more than 5,000 people to date. The PTI Fact Check Desk received four such videos, claimed to be related to earthquakes in Turkiye and Syria, but found in its investigation that they were old and unrelated to the recent calamity in both middle east countries. The social media posts that shared these videos were misleading. Let's have a look at the four claims: Claim 1 A Twitter user shared a 45-second video of a building collapse, claiming to be of the earthquake that hit Turkiye on Feb 6. "February 6, 2023… There are reports of several hundred dead. The Entire buildings collapsed in South #Turkiye the epicenter of 7.8 magnitude earthquake in last hour, #Turkiye #earthquake (Sic)," read the tweet dated Feb 6, which garnered over 400K views, nearly 1000 likes, and over 640 retweets. Here are the links to the tweet and its archive post , and below is the screenshot of the same: Investigation – Claim 1 The Desk started its investigation with an InVid Tool search on the video, followed by a Google Reverse Image search on the six keyframes provided in the results. The Desk found a YouTube video posted on Oct 30, 2020, which carried the same video. The video headline posted by O Tempo – a verified channel – read: "Prédio desaba durante terremoto na Turquia". The Portuguese title translated to English as: "Building collapses during an earthquake in Turkiye." When translated to English, the video's description read: "A strong earthquake of magnitude 7.0 hit the Aegean Sea on Friday (30) and was felt in Greece and Turkiye, where some buildings collapsed in the coastal province of Izmir. At least six people died, and 120 were injured, according to Turkish disaster management authorities." Here is the link to the YouTube video , and below is its screenshot: The Desk also compared the visuals of the two videos – one shared in Twitter post and the other on YouTube – and found them to be the same. Taking a cue from the YouTube video, the Desk conducted a Google search with the keyword "Turkey earthquake October 2020". The search results led the Desk to a report by The Guardian, posted on Oct 30, 2020. The report, titled "Turkey earthquake footage captures moment building collapses in İzmir – video," carried the same video as shared in social media post. Here is the link to the report , and below is its screenshot: In its report dated Oct 31, 2020, CNN carried the same visuals as in the video shared in the Twitter post. Here is the link to the report titled "Powerful earthquake jolts Turkey and Greece, killing at least 27", and below is the screenshot of the same: Subsequently, the Desk concluded that an old video of an earthquake that hit Turkiye's Aegean region in October 2020 was recently shared, falsely relating it to the Feb 6 earthquakes that hit Turkiye and Syria. Claim 2 A verified Twitter user shared a video claiming that a nuclear plant exploded in Turkiye because of the 7.8-magnitude earthquake. "Nuclear plant explodes during the earthquake in Turkey," read the tweet dated Feb 6, which over 3,300 people have viewed. Here are the links to the tweet and its archive post , and below is its screenshot: Investigation – Claim 2 The Desk conducted an InVid Tool search on the video, which provided a few keyframes. A separate Google Reverse Image search on one of them led the Desk to a tweet by a verified handle named CBK News. The tweet dated Feb 6, which garnered over 1 million views, carried the same 5-second video and read: "BREAKING: Nuclear plant explode due to #Earthquake in #Turkiye. Not confirmed Is this real? Leave a comment Follow @CBKNEWS121 #PrayForTurkiye #TurkiyeEarthquake #deprem #Tsunami #Syria." Here are the links to the tweet and its archive post , and below is its screenshot: Continuing the investigation, the Desk conducted a Google search with the keyword "Beirut explosion August 2020" and found a YouTube report by Sky News, posted on Aug 4, 2020. The video's title read: "RAW VIDEO: Beirut blast caught on camera". Here is the link to the video , and below is its screenshot: The Desk also compared the visuals of the two videos – one shared in Twitter post and the other on YouTube – and found them to be the same. The Desk also found a report by Al Jazeera dated Aug 04, 2022, on the second anniversary of the blast in Beirut. According to the report, the "massive explosion in the Port of Beirut ripped through Lebanon's capital, killing 218 people, injuring 7,000, and leaving 300,000 displaced." "A fire at the Beirut port caused the detonation of 2,750 tonnes of ammonium nitrate, which had been improperly stored in a port warehouse for six years," the report mentioned. Here is the link to the report , and below is the screenshot of the same: The Desk noticed that the user posted an update on the Twitter thread hours later and mentioned that the video dated back to August 2020 from Beirut. Here is the link to the tweet , and below is its screenshot: Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the video dated back to August 2020 of a blast in Beirut, falsely linked to the Feb 6 earthquakes in Turkiye and Syria. Claim 3 Another Twitter user shared a video of water flooding into a city and claimed that it showed Tsunami hitting the Turkiye-Syria coastline following the earthquake. "Tsunami hits Turkey-Syria coastline," read the tweet dated Feb 6, which garnered 888 views to date. Here are the links to the tweet and its archive post , and below is the screenshot of the same: Investigation – Claim 3 The Desk conducted an InVid Tool search on the video and found a few keyframes. A separate Google Reverse Image search on one of them led us to a report by Reuters which carried an image similar to the visuals of the video shared in a Twitter post. The caption of the photo read: "A file combination photograph shows the same location on the street in Miyako, Iwate Prefecture, northeastern Japan on two different dates, March 11, 2011 (top) and February 17, 2012 (bottom). REUTERS/Miyako City Office/Handout via Reuters/Files". Here is the link to the report , and below is the screenshot of the same: The Desk compared the visuals of the photo in the article and the visuals of the video and found them to be the same. Taking a cue from this, the Desk conducted a keyword search on Google and found a YouTube video dated Feb 4, 2014. The 14:49-minute video was an extended version of the one shared in the Twitter post and showed similar visuals at 6:01 minutes. Here is the link to the YouTube video titled "Japan Tsunami 2011," and below is its screenshot: The Desk also found a video posted by the official YouTube channel of the Associated Press Mar 14, 2011. "Dramatic new pictures have emerged of a tsunami wave smashing into the Japanese town of Miyako on Friday. The wave crashes over the seawall carrying away everything in its path, including cars and boats. (March 13)," read the caption. Here is the link to the video , and below is the screenshot of the same: The Desk concluded that a 12-year-old video clip of a tsunami that hit Japan's Miyako in 2011 was shared as recent, falsely relating it to the Feb 6 earthquakes. "On March 11, 2011, a massive earthquake – often referred to as the Great East Japan Earthquake – struck off Japan's coast, triggering a towering tsunami that reached land within a half hour," reported AP, adding that it claimed more than 18,000 lives. Claim 4 A Twitter user shared a video of two apartment buildings collapsing and claimed that the visuals were related to the Feb 6 earthquake in Turkiye. "Horrifying video coming from Turkiye. Prayers for Turkiye," read the caption of the Twitter video dated Feb 6, which has garnered over 52K views. Here are the links to the tweet and its archive post and below is the screenshot of the same- Investigation As done in the above claims, the Desk again started the investigation with an InVid Tool search on the video, which provided a few keyframes. A Google Reverse Image search on one of them led the Desk to a report by The Washington Post dated June 30, 2021, which carried the same video. The headline read: "Video timeline: How the Miami-Dade condo collapsed." "A video filmed roughly 300 feet away captures the moment of collapse. First published on Twitter by journalist Andy Slater, the video appears to show the northern section of the building fold onto itself first, quickly followed by the ocean-facing eastern tower," read the portion of the article detailing the video. Here is the link to the article , and below is its screenshot: The Desk also found an article by NBC News carrying the same video. The report dated June 24, 2021, was titled: "4 dead, 11 hurt, dozens missing in high-rise collapse near Miami Beach, officials say". Here is the link to the article , and below is its screenshot: The Washington Post article, published six days after the mishap, reported: "A 12-story condo building on the beachfront in Surfside, Fla., partially collapsed early Thursday morning, killing at least 18 people. More than 145 others remained unaccounted for on Friday, more than a week after the building collapsed." The Desk also compared the visuals of the two videos – one shared in Twitter post and the other carried in The Washington Post article – and found them to be same. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that a video of a building collapse in Miami, Florida, dating back to June 2021, was shared as recent in social media posts, claiming it to be from the Feb 6 earthquakes that hit Turkiye and Syria. The detailed investigation proved that all four video clips shared relating them to the recent earthquakes in Syria and Turkiye were old and shared with a false claims.

title: PTI Fact Check: 2017 video of huge swarm of blackbirds hovering in sky falsely linked to Turkiye earthquakes
content: New Delhi, Feb 08 (Abhinav Gupta / Pratyush Ranjan PTI Fact Check ): A Twitter user shared a video of a huge swarm of blackbirds flying across a road claiming the birds showed 'strange behaviour' just before the devastating Feb 6 earthquakes in Turkiye, where 9000 people were killed. The PTI Fact Check Desk found in its investigation that the video was old and captured the blackbirds' activities in Houston in 2017. The social media post shared the old video with a false claim. Claim A Twitter user posted a video of a swarm of birds flying across a road and claimed that the phenomenon was observed in Turkey before the earthquakes on Feb 6. "Its seismic weapon #earthquake didn't seem Natural Strange behaviour (of objects, Birds, animals) was observed before the earthquake in #Turkey. #Turkey #earthquake #earthquakeinturkey #TurkeyEarthquake #PrayForTurkey #deprem (sic)," read the tweet, which garnered over 39K views and 100 likes. Here are the links to the post and archive post , and below is the screenshot. Investigation The Desk started the investigation with an InVid Tool search on the video, which provided a few keyframes. A Google Reverse Image search on one of them led us to another Twitter post carrying the same video with a similar claim. Here are the links to the tweet and its archive post , and below is the screenshot of the same: The Desk scanned the comment sections of the two Twitter posts and noticed that several users had claimed that the video was old and unrelated to the Feb 6 earthquakes in Turkey. Taking a cue from this, the Desk conducted a keyword search on Google and found an article published on Jan 26, 2017, which carried the same video. The headline of the article read: "What the flock? Eerie video shows a huge swarm of blackbirds hovering in the sky above a Houston freeway." Here is the link to the report and below is the screenshot- The report stated that "the eerie video shows the moment thousands of blackbirds descended upon travellers along a freeway in Houston, Texas, USA." We compared the two videos – one shared in the Twitter post and the other carried by Daily Mail – and found them to be exact. The Desk then conducted a Google search using the keywords "Houston birds video 2017" and found an article by The Sun dated Jan 26, 2017, which carried the same video. The article's headline read: "REAL LIFE HITCHCOCK Terrifying moment sky turns BLACK with a massive murder of crows in scenes that look straight out of Alfred Hitchcock's horror movie 'The Birds' ". Here are the links to the report and archive report , and below is a screenshot for the same. "Spooky screeching and the fluttering of wings can be heard as the birds begin thronging around the highway in Houston, in the US," the report stated. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the video dated back to 2017 and was shot in Houston, Texas. It was recently shared in social media posts, relating it to the Feb 6 earthquakes in Turkiye and Syria.

title: PTI Fact Check: Video of Sidharth Malhotra and Kiara Advani dancing not from their pre-wedding party; details inside
content: New Delhi, Feb 08 (Abhinav Gupta / Pratyush Ranjan PTI Fact Check ): A Twitter user shared a video of actors Sidharth Malhotra and Kiara Advani dancing at an event, claiming that it was from their pre-wedding celebrations in Rajasthan's Jaisalmer. The PTI Fact Check Desk found in its investigation that the video was from the 2020 wedding reception of Advani's cousin Anissa Malhotra. The video was shared as recent in social media posts with a false claim. Claim A Twitter user shared a video of actors Sidharth Malhotra and Kiara Advani dancing at an event, claiming it was from their pre-wedding party in Jaisalmer. Here are the links to the post and archive post , and below is a screenshot of the same- \ The tweet posted on Feb 6 garnered 37.9K views and 134 likes. The text in the tweet read: "The newly wedding couple #Kiara Advani & #SidharthMalhotra #SidharthKiaraWedding #SidKiaraWedding #SidKiaraKiShaadi # #KiaraSidharthwedding.(sic)." Investigation The Desk started its investigation with an InVid Tool search on the video, which provided a few keyframes. A Google search on one of the keyframes led the Desk to a YouTube video titled "sid& Kiara Advani Sadi se phle (Sid and Kiara before their wedding) from the same event posted on Feb 7 with a similar claim. Here are the links to the video and its archive post , and below is the screenshot for the same. The search results also led the Desk to a YouTube video dated Feb 10, 2020, posted by Bollywood Bai – a verified YouTube channel. The video – titled "Sidharth Malhotra & GF Kiara Advani Dance TOGETHER At Party INSIDE Video LEAKED" – carried similar visuals as the Twitter video. Here is the link to the YouTube video , and below is its screenshot: The Desk then compared the visuals of the two videos – one shared on Twitter and the other posted on YouTube – and found them to be the same. The desk then conducted a Google search for the keyword "Anissa Malhotra wedding reception" and found a news report by DNA India titled "Watch: Kiara Advani, Sidharth Malhotra's chemistry dancing at Armaan Jain wedding is undeniable". The report dated Feb 9, 2020, carried the same video posted on Feb 8, 2020, from the Instagram handle of Bollywood photographer Viral Bhayani, which has over 4 lakh views. Here is the link to the report , and below is a screenshot of the same- Here is Bhayani's Instagram post carried in the article, and below is its screenshot: Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the video in the Twitter post claimed as recent from Sidharth and Kiara's pre-wedding celebrations was an old one dating back to February 2020.

title: PTI Fact Check: Old, unrelated photos shared on social media in name of Feb 6 Turkiye-Syria earthquakes; Details inside
content: New Delhi, Feb 08 (Abhinav Gupta / Pratyush Ranjan PTI Fact Check ): Following the devasting Feb 6 earthquakes in Tukiye and Syria, many heart-wrenching photos and videos were shared on social media claiming to be related to the calamity in two middle east countries. The PTI Fact Check Desk received five images on its Fact Check WhatsApp No. +91-8130503759 and found in its investigation that four pictures were old and unrelated to the Feb 6 quakes, while one was an original image. The Desk received four photos posted in one tweet and the fifth photo in another post. Below are the results of the fact-check investigation on all five images: Claim 1 – Dog Sitting on Rubble A Twitter user shared four photos in his post, and the first picture showed a dog sitting on the rubble next to what looks like a child's hand. "Saddest pictures on internet today #Turkey #PrayForTurkey #Turkiye #Tsunami #Syria #earthquakeinturkey (Sic)," read the post published on Feb 7 that garnered over 205K views and 400 retweets. Here are the links to the tweet and its archive post , and below is the screenshot of the same- Investigation – Claim 1 The Desk started the investigation with a Google Reverse Image search on the photo, leading us to another tweet carrying the same photo. The user claimed that the photo was of the dog rescuing a person and used the hashtags earthquake and Turkiye. "Imagen de un perro rescatando a una persona se hace viral #Sismo #Turquía Los mexicanos recordamos a #Frida perrita rescatista de la @SEMAR_mx," the user wrote in the tweet dated Feb 6, which received over 825K views, 15000 likes and was retweeted 3000 times. When translated to English, the caption in Spanish read: "Image of a dog rescuing a person goes viral #Earthquake #Turkey Mexicans remember #Frida rescue dog from the @SEMAR_mx." Here are the links to the tweet and its archive post , and below is the screenshot of the same- The Desk subsequently found a report by the 'A-Z Animals' website published on Sep 12 last year featuring the same photo with the title: "The 10 Best Search and Rescue Dog Breeds". Here is the link to the article , and below is its screenshot: The Desk noticed that the image credits were given to "Noska Photo/Shutterstock.com." Taking a cue from this, the Desk conducted a keyword search on Google and found that the same photo was available on iStock by Getty Images. According to the iStock description, the photo was uploaded on Jan 04, 2019 – over four years before the earthquakes hit Turkiye and Syria on Feb 6, 2023. Here is the link to the iStock page , and below is the screenshot of the same: However, the stock photos website Alamy mentioned that the photo was taken on Oct 18, 2018. It captioned the image as "Dog looking for injured people in ruins after the earthquake." Here is the link to the Alamy page , and below is its screenshot: Below is a combination of the two photos - the one shared in the Twitter post and the other on the Alamy page. While the Desk could not establish this photo's original date of publication, it was found that it's not related to the Feb 6 earthquakes in Turkiye and Syria. Claim 2 – Crying Boy To investigate the second photo in the tweet, which showed a boy sitting on the rubble and crying, the Desk conducted a Google Reverse Image Search and found the same picture on the Shutterstock website with the headline, "Boy crying among the ruins." Here is the link to the Shutterstock page , and below is the screenshot of the same: Below is the combination of both pictures – the one shared in the Twitter post and the other found on Shutterstock. The Desk found several other photos of the child with a man, which were captioned as "father and son among the ruins of a destroyed building." One of the photos can be viewed here , and below are the screenshots of the same: The photos were credited to Zapylaieva Hanna, a Ukrainian photographer. Here is the link to her profile on InSearch . Continuing its search, the Desk found an article by a website named A3, which carried the same photo in November 2020. The report related the image to Turkey's Izmir region's Oct 30, 2020 earthquake. Here is the link to the article and below is its screenshot: The source and publishing date couldn't be found, but it was clear that this photo was not related to the Feb 6 earthquakes in Turkiye and Syria. Claim 3 – Crying, Old Man The third image in the tweet showed an old man crying while carrying loaves of bread in his hand, standing in front of a damaged building. A customised Google search led us to a tweet dated Feb 6 with the same photo. "May Allah grant them better than what they've lost," read the tweet, which has garnered over 1 million views, over 37K likes, and 12000 retweets. Here are the links to the tweet and its archive post , and below is its screenshot: A Google Reverse Image search on the photo in a viral tweet took the Desk to a report by CNN Turk dated Nov 23 last year. The title of the article in Turkish, when translated to English, read: "LAST MINUTE: Same fear after 23 years in Düzce!". The article reported the 6.1-magnitude earthquake that hit the town of Duzce in northern Turkey on Nov 23, 2022. However, it referred to the 7.2-magnitude earthquake that occurred in the same area on Nov 12, 1999, which killed more than 17,000 people. Here is the link to the article and below is its screenshot: Below is a combination of the two photos – the first shared in the Twitter post and the second carried by CNN Turk. The Desk also found an article by a Turkish website T24, which related the photo of the crying older man to the 1999 Düzce Earthquake. The title of the article in Turkish, when translated to English, read: "It's been 20 years since the Düzce Earthquake | Experts warn: Reconstruction peace normalizes illegal construction". Here is the link to the article dated Nov 12, 2019 and below is its screenshot: Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the photo of a crying older man carrying loaves of bread was old and unrelated to the Feb 6 earthquakes in Turkey and Syria. Claim 4 – Crying Woman The Desk started the investigation on the fourth and final photo in the tweet – a woman in hijab kneeling and crying while being consoled by another woman. A Google Reverse Image search on the picture led the Desk to a tweet that carried the same photo relating to Feb 6 earthquakes. "May Allah Protect Our Brothers and Sisters. Prayers For Turkiye, Syria, And All Other Countries Affected By the Earthquake. Powerful 7.8 #PrayersForTurkey," read the caption of the tweet dated Feb 6, which nearly 1,000 people have viewed. Here are the links to the tweet and its archive post , and below is its screenshot: Investigation – Claim 4 The Desk again conducted a Google Reverse Image Search on the photo and found it was shared by Getty Images, with credit to photographer Esra Hacioglu Karakaya. The image's description read: "DIYARBAKIR, TURKIYE - FEBRUARY 06: A woman cries as personnel conduct search and rescue operations in Diyarbakir, Turkiye after 7.7 and 7.6 magnitude earthquakes hits Turkiye's Kahramanmaras, on February 06, 2023. Turkiye's disaster and Emergency Management Authority (AFAD) said the 7.7 magnitude quake struck at 4.17 a.m. (0117GMT) and was centred in the Pazarcik district and 7.6 magnitude quake struck in the Elbistan district in the province of Kahramanmaras in the south of Turkiye. The earthquakes heavily affect Gaziantep, Sanliurfa, Diyarbakir, Adana, Adiyaman, Malatya, Osmaniye, Hatay, and Kilis provinces. (Photo by Esra Hacioglu Karakaya/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images)" Here is the link to the Getty Images page , and below is its screenshot: Also, the Desk could not find any previous reference to the photo over the Internet. Claim 5 – Damaged Building The Desk received another photo on its Fact Check WhatsApp No. +91-8130503759 with a request to verify if it was related to the Feb 6 earthquakes in Turkiye and Syria. A Google Reverse Image Search on the image led us to the Associated Press photo archive website, which published the same photo in context with the 2020 earthquake in Turkiye. "Rescuers work on a collapsed building after a strong earthquake struck Elazig in eastern Turkey, Saturday, Jan. 25, 2020. The earthquake rocked eastern Turkey on Friday, causing some buildings to collapse and killing scores of people, Turkish officials said. (IHA via AP)," read the caption of the photo. Here is the link to the page , and below is its screenshot: Below is a comparison of the two photos – one received on WhatsApp and the other on the AP photo archive website. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that the photo related to the earthquake in the Elazig province of eastern Turkiye in 2020. Following an investigation into the five photos, the Desk found four were old and unrelated to the Feb 6 earthquakes that hit Turkiye and Syria, killing more than 8,000 people. However, one was found to be genuine and related to the calamity.

title: PTI Fact Check: Sadhguru's photo with his daughter Radhe shared on social media portraying him in bad light
content: New Delhi, Feb 09 (Abhinav Gupta / Pratyush Ranjan PTI Fact Check ): A Twitter user shared a photo of spiritual guru Sadhguru Jaggi Vasudev with a woman, questioning his conduct. The PTI Fact Check Desk found in its investigation that the woman in the photo was Sadhguru's daughter Radhe Jaggi. The image displayed the father-daughter bond but was given a tasteless spin in social media posts to portray the spiritual leader in a bad light. Claim A Twitter user shared a photo of Sadhguru Jaggi Vasudeva with a woman seated on his lap. The user questioned the spiritual leader's conduct in his post shared with the image. "बाबा रामदेव के हिसाब से ये #संस्कारी बाबा है एक झलक आप सभी संस्कारी बाबा कि ये तस्वीर देखें! (According to Baba Ramdev, this is #SanskariBaba, a glimpse of this Sanskari Baba for all of you!)," read the tweet dated Feb 6, which has garnered over 1,300 views to date. Here are the links to the tweet dated Feb 6 and its archive post , and below is its screenshot. Investigation The Desk started the investigation with a Google Reverse Image search on the photo. The search results led the Desk to two more tweets with the same picture and the claim. The tweets can be viewed here and here , and their archive posts can be viewed here and here . Below is the combined image of the screenshots of all three tweets- The combined views of all three tweets were almost 100,k with hundreds of retweets and shares on Twitter. The Desk went through the comment sections of these Twitter posts and noticed that several users had mentioned the woman as Sadhuru's daughter Radhe Jaggi. Taking a cue from this, the Desk conducted a keyword search on Google, which led us to the Instagram page of Radhe Jaggi, a verified handle with over 140K followers. The Desk scanned the page and found that Radhe Jaggi had made several posts about her father. One of the recent posts appearing on the page was a post by Sadhgur's official Instagram account, which tagged Radhe Jaggi. "Sadhguru and Radhe Share a Tender Moment at Vijji Maa's Samadhi @radhejaggi #Sadhguru #Vijji #MahaSamadhi #Thaipusam," read the post dated Feb 5. Here is the link to the Instagram post , and below is its screenshot: The Desk conducted a Google search about 'Vijji Maa' mentioned in the Instagram post and found that she was Sadhguru's wife and Radhe Jaggi's mother, who attained Mahasamadhi in 1997. The Desk found a post on Sadhguru's Instagram page, which carried an old photo of the spiritual guru with his wife. Here is a link to the post , and below is its screenshot: The Desk continued its search and found a Facebook post on a Joyful Life page. It carried the same photo shared in tweets in a collage form with another older image of the father and daughter. Here is a link to the Facebook post , and below is the screenshot of the same: We also found a YouTube video in which Radhe responds to a query on whether she will carry forward Sadhguru's legacy. "That one's not true, which I think many people don't understand is that who my father is as Sadhguru is not something that can be carried forward as a legacy just because I am his daughter. I am very wary of using that word in front of anybody because that's not the nature of the work in the ashram…" she responds. Here is the link to the video , and below is the screenshot of the same:

title: PTI Fact Check: Fake quote wrongly attributed to novelist Salman Rushdie shared in social media post
content: New Delhi, Feb 08 (Abhinav Gupta / Pratyush Ranjan PTI Fact Check ): A Twitter user shared a photo attributing a quote to Indian-origin British-American novelist Salman Rushdie that warns other religions and cultures about Islam. In its investigation, the PTI Fact Check Desk found that Rushdie never made any such comments, and he clarified that the quote wasn't his in one of his posts on Twitter. Claim A Twitter user shared a post with a picture of novelist Salman Rushdie on Feb 7, in which the latter was allegedly quoted as saying, "The large majority of peaceful Muslims don't matter because I was attacked by just one Muslim who followed Quran. All religions are different because they have not codified death to whoever doesn't believe in their religion. On my life I want to warn the world that Islam will not rest till every other society, culture and religion is either annihilated or converted. (sic)" The tweet, posted in reply to another tweet, garnered over 6.15 lakh views and 127 likes. Here are the links to the post and archive post , and below is the screenshot- Investigation Starting the investigation, the Desk conducted a Google Reverse Image search on the photo shared in the tweet and noticed that the same user had posted the same photo earlier that day. Here are the links to the post and archive post , and below is the screenshot. Continuing the investigation, the Desk found several users commented that Rushdie never made the remark highlighted in the tweet. Meanwhile, the Google Reverse Image Search results led us to a tweet by Rushdie where he denied making the statement posted on Twitter. "Fake quote. Not said by me," read Rushdie's tweet, posted on Feb 7, which has so far received over 5.95 lakh views and 5,900 likes. Here are the links to the post and archive post , and below is the screenshot- In the next part of the investigation, the Desk conducted a Google search with the keywords "Salman Rushdie anti-Islamic remark" but couldn't find any authentic news report that claimed Rushdie made any such remark as claimed in the tweet. Subsequently, the Desk concluded that Rushdie never remarked as claimed in the tweet and was misquoted in the post. On August 12, 2022, a man stabbed novelist Salman Rushdie multiple times as he was about to give a public lecture at the Chautauqua Institution in Chautauqua, New York, United States. Here is the link to the NY Times article , and below is the screenshot. Rushdie, 75, was blinded in the right eye in the attack, and his left hand was severely injured.

title: PTI Fact Check: Old and edited photo of Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina shared with false claim in social media posts
content: New Delhi, Feb 10 (Abhinav Gupta / Pratyush Ranjan PTI Fact Check ): A Facebook user shared a photo of Bangladesh prime minister Sheikh Hasina purportedly with a dash of vermilion powder on her forehead, claiming her to be a 'religious trader'. The PTI Fact Check Desk found in its investigation that an old photo from Hasina's 2012 visit to India was digitally altered and shared on social media with a false claim. Claim A Facebook user shared two photos of Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina with a post written in Bangla. In the first image, she was seen in a Muslim hijab, and the second picture showed her with a dash of vermillion powder on her forehead. The Facebook post published on Jan 27 this year garnered over 50 reactions and more than ten shares. The English translation of the text written in Bangla read: "People know very well who are religious traders." Here are the links to the post and the archive post . Below is the screenshot of the page- Investigation The Desk started the investigation with a Google Reverse Image Search on the second photo and found the same image was shared in another Facebook post in Bangla published in 2016 and received over 9,000 reactions and 2.7 lakh comments. Here are the links to the post and the archive post . Below is the screenshot of the page. Continuing the investigation, the Desk found a 2012 report by The New Indian Express titled "Sheikh Hasina in India", which had multiple images from Hasina's visit to Agartala in the same year. We noticed one of the photos by the AP news agency had a striking resemblance to the photo shared in Facebook posts. Here are the links to the report and its archive post . Below is the screenshot of the image- The Desk made a combined image of the screenshots of both photos – the one in the 2012 report and the other shared in the Facebook post in 2023 and noticed that the faces behind Hasina were the same in both photos. The dash of vermillion powder and the lady in the red dress was not present in the original image. The Desk subsequently concluded that Hasina's photos shared in the recent Facebook posts were old and edited.

title: PTI Fact Check: Report taking dig at Pakistan shared by Pak-Canadian journalist on Twitter was satire article by parody website
content: New Delhi, Feb 10 (Abhinav Gupta / Pratyush Ranjan PTI Fact Check ): Pakistani-Canadian journalist Tarek Fatah shared on Twitter a screenshot of a report allegedly saying, 'Pakistan will not ask earthquake-hit Turkiye for loans until next month'. The PTI Fact Check Desk found in its investigation that the headline and description in the screenshot were part of a satire article posted on a parody website. The Pakistani-Canadian journalist shared the screenshot of the satire article from his Twitter handle. Claim Pakistani-Canadian journalist Tarek Fatah shared on Twitter a screenshot of an article, which claimed that Pakistan would help earthquake-hit Turkiye by not asking it for loans until next month. "To help earthquake hit Turkiye, Pakistan to not ask Turkiye for loans until next month," read the headline of the article in the screenshot shared in tweet dated Feb 8. "Pakistan is coming forward to help Turkiye by promising not to ask Ankara for loans until next month," wrote Fateh in his tweet, which has garnered over 1.3 million views, 18000 likes and 2700 retweets to date. Here are the links to the tweet and its archive post and below is its screenshot- Investigation Starting its investigation, the Desk noticed in the screenshot that the article was posted by 'Fauxy' on Feb 7. Taking a cue from this, the Desk conducted a Google search for the keyword "Pakistan Turkiye loans, Fauxy", which led us to the article whose screenshot was shared in the Twitter post. Here are the links to the article and its archive post and below is the screenshot of the same: The Desk then scanned the website and found that its 'About Us' page mentioned it as an "entertainment website". "Content of The Fauxy is created by a group of individuals who are well known for producing humorous and entertaining content which keeps going viral online on a daily basis, particularly on social media websites. Content of the Fauxy is original and purely for entertainment purpose," it stated. Here is the link to the page and below is its screenshot- The Desk then conducted another Google search for the keyword "Pakistan to not take loans from Turkiye" to verify the veracity of the claim made in the article and social media post. However, we could not find any authentic report carrying any news. In the meanwhile, the Desk came across a PTI report carried by Business Standard on Feb 9, which quoted Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif saying that it was embarrassing for him to seek more loans from friendly countries, and that it was not a permanent solution for the cash-strapped country's economic challenges. Here is the link to the report and below is its screenshot: The Desk then conducted a customised Google search with the query "Has Pakistan taken any loans from Turkiye?" The search results led us to a report by Arab News, dated Nov 26 last year, with the title: "Pakistan signs €150 million loan agreement with ECO Trade and Development Bank in Turkiye". Here is the link to the article and below is its screenshot: "The Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) Trade and Development Bank on Saturday signed an agreement with Pakistan in Istanbul to provide a soft loan of €150 million for flood relief efforts and support import of fuel by the South Asian country," the report stated. Continuing with its search, the Desk also came across a report by News18 dated Feb 8, which was titled: "Money for Nothing: In Dire Straits, Pakistan Finds Itself on A Tight Leash with IMF". The report deep-dived into the loans taken by Pakistan from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) since 1958, just a decade after the country's creation in 1947 as an independent country. Here is the link to the article and below is its screenshot: Grappling under the aftermath of earthquakes, Turkiye recently cancelled Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif's visit, saying it was "busy in the earthquake rescue and relief operations". Here is the link to the report and below is its screenshot: Subsequently, the Desk concluded that Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif never made any such announcement of not taking any loans from Turkiye, in order to help the earthquake-hit country.

title: PTI Fact Check: No, Rahul Gandhi not with Hindenburg Research founder in this photo; Social media post shared with false claim
content: New Delhi, Feb 12 (Abhinav Gupta / Pratyush Ranjan PTI Fact Check ): A photo of Rahul Gandhi with a person was shared in a recent tweet, claiming the Congress leader was with Hindenburg Research founder Nathan Anderson. Hindenburg Research was in the news for publishing a report accusing the Adani Group of massive stock manipulation. The Gautam Adani-led conglomerate significantly suffered in terms of its valuation and faced criticism from the opposition since January 24, when the US-based short-seller published its report. The Twitter user shared the photo to claim that the Hindenburg Research founder had connections with Rahul Gandhi. In its investigation, The PTI Fact Check Desk found that the person with Rahul Gandhi in the photo was not Nathan Anderson. The claim in the social media post was false. Claim A Twitter user shared a photo of Rahul Gandhi with a person, claiming he was Hindenburg Research Nathan Anderson. The Tweet text posted in Hindi read: "रिश्ता गोरों से सदियों व पुश्तों पुराना है..! ये पप्पू कांग्रेस के युवराज के साथ खड़े हैं महाशय हिडनबर्ग के चीफ 'नाथन ऐन्डर्सन ' हैं..दलाली की कीमत तो जरूर चुकानी होगी. अब कुछ समझाना है आपको या समझे अडानीखेल (Sic)". ("The relation with whites is centuries and generations old..! Mr. Hindenburg's chief 'Nathan Anderson' is with this 'Pappu' crown prince of Congress. The price of brokerage will definitely have to be paid. Did you understand something or you got the sense of Adani Khel".) The tweet was published on Feb 8 and garnered over 240 views and 30 retweets. Here are the link and the archive link to the post. Below is the screenshot of the page. Investigation The desk started its investigation with a Google Reverse Image Search on the photo shared in the tweet and found a report by NDTV published on August 23, 2018. The report's headline read: "Rahul Gandhi Meets German Minister, Discusses Kerala Floods". The Desk noticed that the photo in the NDTV report was similar to the one shared in the recent tweet. We scanned the report to know who was the person with Rahul Gandhi in the lead image and found he was Germany's the-then minister of state at the federal foreign office, Niels Annen. The Desk subsequently found Niels Annen's tweet in which the German minister shared his photo with Rahul Gandhi on August 22, 2018. "Honored to receive @INCIndia president @RahulGandhi in my constituency #Eimsbüttel in Hamburg. India 🇮🇳 is a valued partner and close friend @AuswaertigesAmt @GermanyDiplo @GermanyinIndia #WillkommenRahulGandhi," the tweet read. Here are the link and the archive link to the post. Below is the screenshot of the page. The report further stated that Gandhi met Niels Annen during his visit to Germany as a part of his diaspora outreach programme ahead of the 2019 Lok Sabha elections. The photo was taken when both leaders met in Eimsbüttel in Hamburg. The Desk subsequently found the same photo shared by the Congress' Twitter handle on Aug 22, 2018. Here is the link to the tweet , and below is the screenshot of the post- The Desk concluded that the person with Rahul Gandhi in the photo was not Hindenburg Research founder Nathan Anderson. He was former German minister Niels Annen, who met Gandhi during his visit to Germany in August 2018.

title: PTI Fact Check: Simulation video shared as real on social media after US fighter jet shot down suspected Chinese balloon
